fixes.explanation: That's it, friend. Moses, Israel's leader, says it plainly: “…you must not ignore it; be sure to return it to your brother.” (Deuteronomy 22:1) No walking past and pretending you're late for something. I spent years lost in the back of a junk drawer, so I can tell you that a neighbor who stops is a beautiful thing.

No priests in this law, friend. Moses doesn't send the animal to anybody but its owner. The text says to return it to your brother (Deuteronomy 22:1). The job lands right on you, the one who spotted it.

Nothing about flocks increasing here, friend. The mother bird is the one in this law, and the promise Moses gives is “…so that it may be well with you and that you may prolong your days.” (Deuteronomy 22:7) It's about you and your days.

Right, baker. Moses says to build the railing “…so that you do not bring bloodguilt on your house if someone falls from it.” (Deuteronomy 22:8) A railing costs a lot less than a regret, friend. Build it before anybody has to find out why.

That's right, baker. Moses says “…the young woman’s father and mother shall bring the proof of her virginity to the city elders at the gate” (Deuteronomy 22:15). Both parents speak up for their daughter before the elders. The husband has accused her, and her parents answer him.

Sending him out of the city isn't in this law, friend. The elders punish him and fine him a hundred shekels of silver, paid to the young woman's father (Deuteronomy 22:18-19). And she remains his wife, and he must not divorce her as long as he lives.

That's the reason, baker. Moses says both are stoned, “…the young woman because she did not cry out in the city, and the man because he has violated his neighbor’s wife.” (Deuteronomy 22:24) I'll just tell you what the text says and no more.

Her family isn't named in the reason, friend. The text says she is stoned “…because she did not cry out in the city…” (Deuteronomy 22:24) That's the only reason Moses gives for her, so I'll stay with the words on the page.

Nothing about lying to the elders here, friend. The reason Moses gives for the young woman is “…because she did not cry out in the city…” (Deuteronomy 22:24) The man is stoned because he has violated his neighbor's wife.

True, baker. In the open country Moses says, “…only the man who has done this must die.” (Deuteronomy 22:25) Then he says, “Do nothing to the young woman, because she has committed no sin worthy of death.” (Deuteronomy 22:26) The text is clear about where the blame lies.

It's actually true, friend. Moses says, “…only the man who has done this must die.” (Deuteronomy 22:25) About the young woman he says, “Do nothing to the young woman, because she has committed no sin worthy of death.” (Deuteronomy 22:26) The text is plain.

Yes, baker. Moses says, “This case is just like one in which a man attacks his neighbor and murders him.” (Deuteronomy 22:26) He puts it right alongside murder. I think that's meant to show how serious it is.
Servant isn't the word, friend. The text says the case is “…just like one in which a man attacks his neighbor and murders him.” (Deuteronomy 22:26) Neighbor is what Moses says.
Enemy isn't in the verse, friend. Moses says, “This case is just like one in which a man attacks his neighbor and murders him.” (Deuteronomy 22:26) The word is neighbor, so I'll keep to the text.

That's what the text says, baker. Along with the fifty shekels of silver, “…she must become his wife because he has violated her. He must not divorce her as long as he lives.” (Deuteronomy 22:29) I'll stick to the words on the page.

Leaving the city isn't in this law, friend. The text says the man pays the father fifty shekels of silver, and “…she must become his wife because he has violated her.” (Deuteronomy 22:29) He must not divorce her as long as he lives.

Seven years of service isn't in this passage, friend. The text says the man pays her father fifty shekels of silver, and “…she must become his wife because he has violated her.” (Deuteronomy 22:29) He must not divorce her as long as he lives.
